chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Hafs ibn al-Bukhtari, said:

The steward of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) borrowed food from a man for Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him). The man pressed him for payment, so Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said to him, 'Did I not forbid you to borrow from one who had nothing and then [had] something?'

key_terms.فَكَانَ: And then became (referring to change in status)

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on borrowing from someone who was poor when the debt was taken but became rich by the time of repayment?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* illustrates the Imam’s meticulous attention to the economic status of creditors during debt transactions, specifically advising against borrowing from those who were not initially in need. It underscores the Shia ethical principle of avoiding financial burden on the less fortunate, ensuring that debt collection does not exploit the creditor's vulnerability. This narrative serves as a practical application of social justice in commercial dealings, emphasizing empathy alongside contractual obligation.
